title: Instruments in the room
hook: harmonium and tabla today, and older strings like the rebab and saranda

segments.voice: Yesterday, raag, the musical mood of every hymn. Your line was music carries meaning. Did one song's mood reach you before its words? Day one hundred six.

During kirtan in a gurdwara, look toward the front, near the Guru Granth Sahib. Often a few musicians sit on a low platform. One or two have a small wooden box in front of them, pumping a bellows at the back with one hand and pressing keys with the other. Another sits behind a pair of drums, fingers flickering. It all looks ancient and timeless. But in Guru Nanak's gatherings, as Sikhs tell it, none of those instruments were there. There was a man with a stringed instrument across his lap. The sounds in the room have changed. What they're for hasn't.
screen: `THREE MUSICIANS AT THE FRONT.` → `A BOX, A BELLOWS, TWO DRUMS.` → `NOT WHAT NANAK HEARD.`

segments.voice: Start with the box. That's the harmonium, a small reed organ. Punjabis often just call it the vaaja. It came to India with Europeans in the nineteenth century, and a hand-pumped version made for sitting on the floor caught on fast. Today it's at the heart of gurdwara kirtan. Beside it, the tabla, a pair of hand drums, keeping the rhythm and the pulse. Now go back further. Guru Nanak's companion Mardana played the rebab, a plucked string instrument, and you met him on day thirty-one. Tradition links other string instruments to later Gurus: the saranda, a bowed instrument, to Guru Arjan; the taus, shaped like a peacock, to Guru Hargobind; the dilruba to Guru Gobind Singh. Before the tabla, the older drum was the jori, a pair played with the hands. In recent years, Sikh musicians and schools have been bringing these string instruments back. Some say the harmonium's fixed notes can't bend the way a raag wants to, and the old strings suit gurbani better. Others love the harmonium, because it's easy to learn and carries a congregation well, and it's how their grandparents sang. Both are heard in gurdwaras today, often side by side. Here's what doesn't change. None of the instruments is the point. The Word is at the center, and every sound in the room is there to carry it. The drum holds the time. The strings or the reeds hold the melody. The voice holds the words. And the sangat holds the listening. Every sound has a part.
screen: `THE HARMONIUM AND THE TABLA.` · `THE REBAB, SARANDA AND TAUS.` · `BRINGING THE STRINGS BACK.` · `EVERYTHING CARRIES THE WORD.` · then, large: `EVERY SOUND HAS A PART.`

segments.voice: Play a recording of kirtan if you can, or any music with a few instruments. Listen once, and pick out just the drum. Follow only that. Then let the drum go and find the melody: the harmonium, or the strings. Follow only that. Then find the voice. Finally, let them all come back together, and hear how each one leans on the others. If there's no music near you, do the same with the sounds of the room. The bell holds the time.
Vaaja. The everyday Punjabi name for the harmonium, now at the heart of gurdwara kirtan alongside the tabla, and the rebab, saranda and taus of the Gurus' time.
Your line: every sound has a part. Today, pick out one sound you usually tune out, a fridge, a bird, a voice, and give it your full attention. Day one hundred six.

howItsDone: Gurdwara kirtan today is often sung with harmonium and tabla, while a growing number of musicians and schools also teach the older string instruments, such as the rebab, saranda, taus and dilruba.

Harmonium: European reed organs arrived in the 19th century; the hand-pumped floor harmonium developed in India (c. 1875). Confirm framing.
